intro: Looking for an office architect near you usually means you have a workplace that no longer fits how your team actually works, or a lease and a floor plan that need rethinking. You want someone local enough to visit the space, understand the building and guide you through design and approvals. iComply is a free introduction service: you tell us what you need, and we introduce you to a suitable UK architecture practice that quotes you directly, with the price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for an office architect usually need
need_lead: Most enquiries come from occupiers and managers trying to make a workplace work better without disrupting the business.
needs: You are reworking an office for hybrid working and need the layout, desks and meeting space to match how people actually use the building.
You have found a new office and want an architect to test whether your fit-out ideas are realistic before you commit to the lease.
Your current space feels noisy, cramped or uncomfortable, and you want acoustics, light and wellbeing designed in rather than patched up later.
You need to know whether your lease allows the alterations you have in mind, and how to plan the work in stages so the team can keep working.
You want help navigating building regulations approval, planning permission or party wall matters that sit alongside the design work.
context: "Architect" is a protected title in the UK. Only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices.

Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, but they are not registered architects, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring. Because your search is for someone near you, it is also sensible to ask how often they will visit the building, since an office fit-out depends on understanding the actual space.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the office you have, including roughly how many people work there and whether you own or lease it.
Explain what is prompting the work, such as a move, a lease renewal, hybrid working or a fit-out that feels out of date.
Say whether you already have floor plans, a survey or a landlord's consent process underway.
Mention any constraints you know about, such as lease restrictions on alterations, listed status or shared building services.
Set out whether you need full design through to completion or just early advice on what is feasible.
Note your preferred location and how far you are willing for the architect to travel to the office.
questions: Are you on the Architects Registration Board register, and can you confirm your professional indemnity insurance?
How will you get to know our building and how often will you visit the office?
Can you help us understand what our lease allows before we plan any alterations?
How would you phase the work so our team can keep working through the fit-out?
What will the written appointment cover, including services, fees and responsibilities?
Which approvals, such as building regulations or planning permission, are likely to be needed for our plans?

faqs.q: Do I need a registered architect for an office fit-out?
faqs.a: Not always, but "architect" is a protected title, so only people on the Architects Registration Board register can use it. Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, so it is worth asking which you are hiring and checking the ARB register before you appoint anyone.

faqs.q: How local does an office architect need to be?
faqs.a: Close enough to visit the building regularly, since understanding the actual space matters for a fit-out. Ask how often they expect to be on site and whether travel is included in their quote.

faqs.q: Can an architect help with lease restrictions on alterations?
faqs.a: They can help you understand what your lease may restrict and how to approach your landlord, though lease terms are a separate matter from design. It is worth raising this early, before plans are drawn up.

faqs.q: What should a written appointment include?
faqs.a: It should set out the services, fees and responsibilities clearly before any work begins. Building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes that your architect can help you navigate.
